title: This Is the Man Whose Footfall Mecca’s Valley Knows
intro: Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani tells of al-Farazdaq answering a question about Ali ibn al-Husayn, known as Zayn al-Abidin, on a pilgrimage attended by the Umayyad prince Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. The reports differ over who asked and who professed ignorance. The poet calls Mecca itself to witness, then follows Ali’s hands and gestures before naming what the wider community owes his family. Abu Tammam’s Hamasa gives six of these verses, including the opening, to al-Hazin al-Kinani. Al-Tabrizi names his patron as Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Malik.

translation: This is the man whose footfall Mecca’s valley knows.
The House knows him, and the ground outside and within its bounds.
1.sharh: Someone in the crowd needs the man identified. The ground under his foot has an answer ready, and the poet calls as witnesses even places that have no voice.

translation: This is a son of the best of all God’s servants.
This is the devout, the pure, the spotless, the man all recognise.
2.sharh: “This” twice supplies the force of a pointing finger. An ancestor gives Ali his lineage, while the string of qualities in the second half belongs to Ali himself.

translation: This is Fatima’s son, if you do not know him.
With his forefather the line of God’s prophets was sealed.
3.sharh: “Son” reaches back beyond one generation. Fatima was Ali’s grandmother and Muhammad his great-grandfather, so her name answers the question through a line the audience knows.

translation: Your saying “Who is this?” can do him no harm.
Arabs and non-Arabs know the man you disown.
4.sharh: The question itself becomes a piece of testimony against its speaker. The two names for peoples are meant to exhaust the world in which a reputation can travel.

translation: Both his hands are relief that reaches everyone.
People look to them for rain, and want never overtakes them.
5.sharh: A rain prayer has been transferred to a pair of open hands. Both give, and the people waiting below them have the same stake in their generosity as a dry country in its clouds.

translation: Gentle by nature, he has no outbursts to fear.
Two things adorn him, a handsome form and fine traits.
6.sharh: Someone approaching him need never anticipate a sudden burst of temper. This explains how the awe he inspires in the crowd can coexist with a character easy to approach.

translation: He takes up the burdens of people weighed down.
His ways are sweet, and “yes” comes sweetly from him.
7.sharh: The burden is heavy on the people who bring it. The answer sounds light on his lips, and the word “sweet” passes from his manner to the actual word a petitioner hopes to hear.

translation: He never said “no” except in his profession of faith.
But for that profession, even his “no” would be “yes”.
8.sharh: The Muslim profession of faith opens with “There is no god but God.” The poet looks for a single occasion on which such a generous man would have to pronounce a negative.

translation: His kindness reached all creatures and swept away
their darkness, their poverty and their want.
9.sharh: The verb is used of a cloud or a bank of darkness lifting. The last two nouns give the darkness a material shape in the lives of people short of necessities.

translation: When Quraysh see him, someone among them says,
“In this man’s noble deeds generosity comes to its height.”
10.sharh: A member of Quraysh gets a speaking part. The people best placed to recognise a fellow Meccan give their own public judgement of what they see.

translation: He lowers his eyes from modesty, others from awe of him.
No one speaks to him until he smiles.
11.sharh: The same movement passes from him to the crowd for two different reasons. His smile then gives silent permission for conversation to begin.

translation: In his hand is a cane, fragrant with the scent
of a commanding man with a proud high nose.
12.sharh: The scent appears to pass from the man into the cane. The high bridge of his nose was also an established physical image for dignity, so the portrait works at two levels.

translation: It almost takes hold of him, knowing his palm,
the corner of the Hatim, when he comes to touch the Stone.
13.sharh: The subject arrives late. A pilgrim normally reaches out to touch the sacred stone, and here the corner almost reaches back in recognition of his palm.

translation: God honoured and exalted him long ago.
For him the Pen ran with that decree on God’s Tablet.
14.sharh: The writing precedes the public scene at Mecca. Divine decree supplies a record of Ali’s standing that no declaration by a prince can revise.

translation: Who among all creatures does not bear at the neck
a favour owed his forebears or the man himself?
15.sharh: A favour carried at the neck is a debt of gratitude. The question allows for obligations inherited from earlier generations as well as those incurred in Ali’s lifetime.

translation: Whoever thanks God thanks this man’s forebears.
The nations received the faith from his house.
16.sharh: The preceding debt now has a history. Peoples far beyond Mecca received a faith first proclaimed by a member of this family, and the poet includes remembrance of the family in giving thanks.

translation: He traces his descent to a summit of faith
beyond the reach of hands or the climbing foot.
17.sharh: A pedigree turns into an ascent. The hand stretching upwards and the foot trying to climb give a physical measure of how far above other claims the poet places this one.

translation: His forefather was the one to whom even prophets yielded precedence.
To the excellence of his community the nations bowed.
18.sharh: Parallel verbs put Muhammad among the prophets and his community among the nations. Ali’s standing is praised by tracing a consequence of his ancestor’s distinction.

translation: His shoot springs from the Messenger of God.
Good are its planting places, his nature and his ways.
19.sharh: Lineage becomes propagation from a living tree. The verse names the quality of the soil and then lets us see what it has produced in Ali’s own temperament.

translation: The cloth of night parts at the light of his brow,
as darkness clears before the shining sun.
20.sharh: Night is first a piece of cloth drawn across one face. The sunrise then enlarges that private radiance until a whole landscape can see by it.

translation: To love his people is faith, to hate them
is unbelief. Near them one finds safety and refuge.
21.sharh: The poet extends his declaration of loyalty to the entire household. The break after “hate them” delays his harshest judgement, followed immediately by the promise of shelter.

translation: After God’s name, their mention comes first
at every opening, and with it speech is brought to a close.
22.sharh: An audience could hear a blessing on Muhammad and his family framing an address. The poet finds their precedence in the order of the words people already use.

translation: If the God-fearing are counted, these are their leaders.
Ask for the best on earth and the answer is “they”.
23.sharh: First comes an imagined roll of the devout, then a question addressed to everyone on earth. At this point a single pronoun suffices to give the family’s name.

translation: No giver can follow so far in their generosity.
No people, however noble, can come near them.
24.sharh: A rival giver and then an entire people try to draw level. The repeated language of distance makes generosity something a person can advance in without ever catching them.

translation: They are the rains when hardship grips,
the lions of al-Shara when battle is at its height.
25.sharh: Rain is what people need from them in a season of want. When the danger changes, the image changes with it, to the lions proverbial for their ferocity.

translation: Hardship takes nothing from the openness of their hands.
It is all one whether they grow rich or go without.
26.sharh: The open hands return under more exacting conditions. The measure of the family’s generosity is what it gives when its own resources run short.

translation: Through love of them people ask that harm and trials be warded off
and kindness and blessings be fostered.
27.sharh: The closing verbs sound like two petitions, first for protection, then for good to be sustained. Their impersonal form leaves room for anyone who shares the devotion to speak them.

1.1.4.head: البَطحاء
1.1.4.meaning: Al-Batha', the gravelly floor of the Meccan valley.

1.1.5.head: وَطأَة
1.1.5.meaning: The footfall or impression left by a step.

1.2.3-4.head: الحِلّ وَالحَرَم
1.2.3-4.meaning: “The unrestricted and the sacred”, the land outside and inside Mecca’s sanctuary.

2.2.5.head: العَلَم
2.2.5.meaning: A conspicuous landmark, hence a person universally recognised.

3.1.3.head: فاطِمَة
3.1.3.meaning: Fatima, daughter of Muhammad, mother of al-Husayn and grandmother of Ali ibn al-Husayn.

4.1.5.head: ضارَ
4.1.5.meaning: Caused harm or diminished someone’s standing.

5.1.3.head: غِياث
5.1.3.meaning: Relief sent to those in distress, suggestive here of welcome rain.

5.2.1.head: اِستَوكَفَ
5.2.1.meaning: Asked for drops to fall, here looked to the two hands for gifts as for rain.

6.1.5.head: بادِرَة
6.1.5.meaning: A hasty act or outburst of temper.

6.2.4.head: الخَلق
6.2.4.meaning: Physical form and appearance, paired here with inward traits.

7.1.5.head: اُفتُدِحَ
7.1.5.meaning: Were weighed down by misfortune. Ibn Khallikan gives a shorter form, fudihu, with the same sense.

7.2.2.head: شَمائِل
7.2.2.meaning: Traits of character apparent in one’s dealings with others.

8.1.7.head: تَشَهُّد
8.1.7.meaning: Tashahhud, the profession of faith recited during prayer, beginning “There is no god but God”.

8.2.4.head: لاء
8.2.4.meaning: His “no”, the word for refusal used as a noun. The poet turns the sentence round and makes “yes” stand in for the refusal a petitioner might expect.

9.2.2.head: غَياهِب
9.2.2.meaning: Deep darknesses, used here of privation.

9.2.3.head: إِملاق
9.2.3.meaning: Penury, the exhaustion of one’s means.

10.1.3.head: قُرَيش
10.1.3.meaning: Quraysh, the Meccan tribe to which Muhammad and his family belonged.

12.1.2.head: خَيزُران
12.1.2.meaning: Khayzuran, a light cane or staff.

12.2.5.head: عِرنين
12.2.5.meaning: The high bridge of the nose.

12.2.6.head: شَمَم
12.2.6.meaning: A high, straight nasal bridge, traditionally associated with distinction.

13.2.1-2.head: رُكن الحَطيم
13.2.1-2.meaning: “The corner of the Hatim”, the sacred corner at which the pilgrim reaches towards the Stone.

13.2.6.head: اِستَلَمَ
13.2.6.meaning: Touched the Black Stone during the circuits of the Kaaba.

14.2.5.head: اللَّوح
14.2.5.meaning: The Tablet on which divine decrees are recorded.

15.1.4-5.head: في رِقابِهِم
15.1.4-5.meaning: “At their necks”, a favour to which they owe a response.

15.2.1.head: أَوَّلِيَّة
15.2.1.meaning: The honoured ancestry and predecessors of a man.

19.1.5.head: نَبعَة
19.1.5.meaning: A shoot of the nab' tree, here a scion or line of descent.

20.1.6.head: غُرَّة
20.1.6.meaning: A bright forehead or the radiant front of the face.

21.2.4.head: مُعتَصَم
21.2.4.meaning: A place of refuge or protection.

23.1.6.head: إِمام
23.1.6.meaning: A leader or exemplar whom others follow.

24.2.2.head: دانى
24.2.2.meaning: Approached another in rank or achievement.

25.2.2-3.head: أُسد الشَّرى
25.2.2-3.meaning: “Lions of al-Shara”, lions named for a place proverbial in descriptions of fierceness.

27.2.1.head: اِستَرَبَّ
27.2.1.meaning: Sought the increase and continuance of a good thing.
